title: Why does the sky look red at sunset?
sources: NOAA National Weather Service Optical Phenomena

lines.text: Why is the sky brilliant blue at noon, but shifts into fiery crimson and orange as the sun sets?
lines.caps: Why do sunsets turn *fiery red | while noon is *blue?

lines.text: The answer is an optical phenomenon called Rayleigh scattering.
lines.caps: Caused by an optical *law | called Rayleigh *scattering

lines.text: Sunlight looks white, but it contains all the colors of the visible rainbow.
lines.caps: Sunlight contains *all colors | of the visible *rainbow

lines.text: Blue light has short, choppy wavelengths that easily scatter in every direction off nitrogen gas molecules at midday.
At sunset, the Sun sits low on the horizon, forcing its rays to travel through ten times more atmosphere to reach your eyes.
lines.caps: At dusk, rays travel *through | ten times more *atmosphere!

lines.text: Most blue and violet light gets scattered away long before reaching you, leaving only long red and orange wavelengths.
lines.caps: Blue scatters away leaving *only | long red and orange *waves

lines.text: You are seeing the longest light wavelengths making it through the atmosphere's marathon run.
lines.caps: The sunset is the *marathon winner | of visible *light!
